title: Mission Beach Tier 4 STRO licenses and the waitlist, explained
excerpt: Every Mission Beach whole-home short-term rental license is taken. How the Tier 4 cap and lottery waitlist work, what frees up a license, and what owners and buyers can do now.

seo.title: Mission Beach Tier 4 STRO License and Waitlist (2026)
seo.description: All Mission Beach Tier 4 STRO licenses are taken. How San Diego's cap, lottery waitlist and 90-day rule work, and what owners can do, as of November 2026.

heroCaption: Mission Beach from above, between the Pacific and Mission Bay. Whole-home short-term rentals here need a Tier 4 license.
bodyHtml:
Mission Beach is the only San Diego community with its own whole-home short-term rental license, Tier 4, and its own cap. As of November 2026 every Tier 4 license is taken and new applicants can only join a waitlist when the city reopens it. This guide explains how the cap and waitlist work, what frees up a license, and what Mission Beach owners and buyers can do in the meantime.

As of November 2026

License counts are the City Treasurer's figures as of November 6, 2026. Counts and waitlist positions change as licenses are issued, so check the city's pages before acting.

What is a Tier 4 STRO license?

Tier 4 is the license a host needs to rent a whole home in the Mission Beach Community Planning Area for more than 20 days a year when the host does not live on site. The rest of the city uses Tier 3 for the same kind of rental. According to the City Treasurer's Short-Term Residential Occupancy page, the number of Tier 4 licenses "will not exceed 30% of the Mission Beach Community Planning Area," a figure based on SANDAG housing estimates last updated in March 2024.

The same page sets the terms that come with the license:

  • Fees: a $41 application fee and a $1,129 license fee, both non-refundable (effective March 1, 2025). Renewal costs the same.
  • Term: licenses expire two years from the date of issue and can be renewed. The city emails a renewal notice 60 days before expiration.
  • Use requirement: the host must rent the home short term for at least 90 days a year during the license term to keep a Tier 3 or Tier 4 license (the page cites §510.0107(c)). The city says the ordinance has no exceptions and that missing the minimum "could result in license revocation."
  • Guest stays: a two-night minimum.

Are any Mission Beach licenses available now?

No. As of November 6, 2026, the Treasurer reported 1,099 Tier 4 licenses issued and none remaining. The page states that both the Tier 4 application period and the Tier 4 waitlist application period are closed. For comparison, Tier 3 had 4,863 licenses issued and 798 remaining on the same date, so a whole-home license outside Mission Beach can still be obtained.

How does the Tier 4 waitlist work?

Applicants are placed on the waitlist in an order set by a random lottery, and the city offers licenses down the list as they become available. Tier 4 applications first opened in October 2022, reached the cap, and closed on November 30, 2022, the city said in its June 2025 announcement. The most recent window ran from July 1 to August 15, 2025. After it closed, the city ran a random lottery among the completed applications to set processing order and waitlist position.

The city's lottery administration rule sets the trigger for the next window: "Once the waitlist reaches 25 applications, the application period will be reopened for 45 days." An independent department then runs a new random lottery to rank the new applications. The Treasurer's page adds that it will post information about accepting Tier 4 applications once the waitlist has been exhausted. The city gives no date.

The waitlist itself is public. The Treasurer posts it as a PDF that lists each position and application number, updated "as changes occur and new licenses become available." The September 15, 2026 version listed 113 positions; a newer version was posted in November. The list shows order, not offers made, so it does not tell an applicant how soon a license will come.

What frees up a Tier 4 license?

A Tier 4 license opens up only when an existing one leaves the pool. The city's rules point to three ways that happens:

  • Expiration without renewal. Licenses run two years and must be renewed.
  • Cancellation. A host who sells must cancel the license, because STRO licenses "are not transferrable." A buyer of a licensed Mission Beach home does not inherit the license; our guide to buying or selling a home with an STRO license covers that hand-off.
  • Revocation. For example, for failing the 90-day use requirement.

The city does not publish how many Tier 4 licenses turn over in a year, so there is no reliable way to estimate wait times from public data.

Who can apply when the waitlist reopens?

A host must be "a natural person with the legal right to occupy the dwelling unit," and a host may hold only one license at a time. Someone who already holds a lower-tier license can apply for Tier 4 but must cancel the existing license before the Tier 4 license is issued, according to the city's 2025 waitlist FAQ. Applications also need a transient occupancy tax certificate and a paid rental unit business tax, and the city will not process them for homes with pending enforcement actions.

What should Mission Beach owners do now?

The answer depends on whether the owner already holds a Tier 4 license.

Owners with a Tier 4 license

While the cap is full, a Tier 4 license that lapses cannot simply be applied for again, so keeping it current matters more here than anywhere else in the city. Track the expiration date, renew when the 60-day notice arrives, and make sure the home is rented at least 90 days a year. A slow season, a long renovation or an extended family stay can push a home below that line. Our STRO and TOT compliance guide covers the tax filings that go with the license.

Owners and buyers without one

Plan on not having whole-home short-term income in Mission Beach until a license is actually issued. The uncapped options are Tier 1 (whole-home rentals of 20 days a year or fewer) and Tier 2 (home sharing in the host's primary residence). Applicants for the next Tier 4 window should watch the city's STRO page for the reopening notice, since the last window lasted 45 days.

Cardo manages licensed homes in Mission Beach and tracks renewals and the 90-day minimum for each one. Owners weighing their options can request a free earning estimate or see current city-wide license counts on our STRO license page.

This article is general information as of November 2026, not tax or legal advice. Confirm current requirements with the City of San Diego Office of the City Treasurer and a qualified professional before applying, buying or selling.
